newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sailor questioned in rape in Japan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sailor questioned in rape in Japan.

text.p: A U.S. Navy sailor was taken into custody at Yokosuka Naval Base in Japan on Wednesday after he allegedly beat and raped a young Japanese woman, Navy officials said at the Pentagon.

The officials, who asked not to be identified, said the petty officer third class was being questioned by the Navy's Criminal Investigative Service after security forces responded to a disturbance at the bachelor's enlisted quarters on the big base.

They said no formal charges were filed immediately in the incident, which could cause new tension in U.S.-Japan relations after the widely publicised 1995 sexual assault of a Japanese schoolgirl on Okinawa by three U.S. servicemen.
The incident also came as U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen prepared to visit Japan and South Korea next week.
One Navy official at the Pentagon said the young woman in Wednesday's incident was found bruised by base security personnel and she apparently suffered a broken collar bone.

"Upon arrival (at the quarters), they found a 21-year-old Japanese woman who had been beaten and allegedly sexually assaulted by an E-4 (third class petty officer) assigned to Yokosuka Naval Computer and Telecommunications Station," the official said.

"She was taken to the U.S. Naval Hospital at Yoksuka where she was treated for a broken clavicle, abrasions and contusions," he official said. "The E-4 was taken into custudy by U.S. naval authorities and he is being questioned by the Naval Criminal Investigative Service."

The official referred all further queries to Navy officials at the base, where a U.S. aircraft carrier and thousands of sailors are stationed as part of a presence of 100,000 U.S. military personnel in the Pacific and Asia.

The United States and Japan in December 1996 finally settled a bitter dispute over U.S. military bases on the southern island of Okinawa, agreeing to cut the American presence there and announcing plans for a revolutionary floating helicopter base off the island.

The agreement was signed by former Defence Secretary William Perry and other top U.S. and Japanese officials at the foreign ministry, culminating a year of negotiations spurred by the September 1995 rape of an Okinawan schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen.
At the time, Tokyo and Washington agreed to move forward quickly with talks on plans to strengthen military cooperation and to impress upon China that the tightening ties will not threaten Beijing.
Also signing that agreement were Japanese Foreign Minister Yokuhiko Ikeda, Defence Minister Fumio Kyuma and U.S. Ambassador to Japan Walter Mondale.

Asked how an agreement which would remove few if any U.S. troops from Japan could assuage Okinawa's bitterness over the rape and the continuing military presence, Ikeda said that it would require a public relations campaign in the nation.
